newsitem.title: USA: IMF official urges small rise in U.S. interest rates.
newsitem.headline: IMF official urges small rise in U.S. interest rates.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official Thursday called on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to help keep inflation in check.
"It's probably about time for a rise in interest rates," IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer told Reuters Financial Television.

He said the U.S. economy has strengthened "quite a bit" and the central bank probably needed to show its resolve to prevent the economy from overheating. He said though that a substantial rate rise was not needed.

The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets on Sept. 24 to plot monetary strategy. Wall Street stock prices surged to near-record levels on Thursday on hopes the Fed may hold off from raising rates.
Fischer was generally upbeat about the outlook for the world economy as a whole. "It looks reasonably good," he told a news conference.
He said that the Japanese economic recovery was "well underway" and forecast growth there next year of 2.7 percent. Until this year, Japan's economy had been mired in a near-recession.

Fischer though signalled out Europe as one potential trouble spot for the world economy in 1997. But he added that he was encouraged by the recent sharp cut in German interest rates, saying it had "really made a difference."
"We don't see a need right now for any further easing (of rates)," Fischer said.

He made it clear that Germany and and its European counterparts need to monitor the situation closely as they strive to meet the tough budget goals in the Maastricht treaty for the launch of European Monetary Union in 1999.
"If the situation were to slow or not develop as well as we hoped, there would be a case for a further easing," he said.

Elsewhere in the world economy, the IMF expects the so-called transition economies of the former communist bloc to register "positive growth" on the whole for the first time since the break-up of the Soviet Union.
"Growth in Africa is picking up," Fischer added. "Growth in Latin America is picking up."
Economic growth in East Asian nations is expected to slow in 1997, but to levels -- seven, eight or nine percent -- that would still be regared as a "gallop" elsewhere in the world, he added.
